transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Aisha Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Hale (OceanCrest CISO), Sofia Martinez (Head of Cloud Infra), Daniel Cho (SecOps)
---
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. This is Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account. We've got Aisha from our security/infra team with me. Marcus, Sofia, Daniel, thanks for joining. Can you hear us ok?
[00:06] Marcus Hale: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Jordan. We're, uh, mainly focused on the Private VPC offering, we want to understand isolation and egress controls, especially since we have regulatory constraints for EU data residency and minimal egress.
[00:16] Aisha Patel: Great — that's exactly what we'll deep-dive on today. Quick agenda: network topology options (VPC peering vs dedicated private link vs on-prem), ingress patterns, egress IP management and firewall rules, how we integrate with customer KMS, RBAC/SSO model, audit logs and retention, and SOC 2 / ISO artifacts. Does that align?
[00:28] Sofia Martinez: Yes, that's perfect. Also would like to understand how Redwood handles outbound calls from the model runtime — like telemetry, updates, and how to prevent accidental outbound to external endpoints.
[00:36] Jordan Lee: Totally -- we'll cover egress controls and allowlist-only options.
[00:40] Aisha Patel: Quick context on how Private works: there are two common patterns we see — private VPC deployment inside the customer's cloud account using a managed control plane, or a fully on-prem bundle where workload and control plane are customer-managed. For VPC we typically provision dedicated subnets and route tables; we can either set up a private link (like AWS PrivateLink) or use peering with strict route tables.
[01:02] Marcus Hale: For us, cloud account deployment is preferred but we need strict network ACLs and egress only through our managed firewall.
[01:08] Aisha Patel: Understood. So typical architecture: Redwood's control plane endpoints are reachable only over a customer-provided private endpoint. Model runtime nodes live in isolated subnets without public IPs; egress is through a centralized NAT/egress appliance you manage. We can give static egress IPs if you assign a NAT gateway with Elastic IPs or use our managed egress pool — but for strict compliance we recommend customer-owned NAT so you retain control.
[01:32] Daniel Cho: Can you clarify managed egress pool — what logs or attestations do you provide if we used Redwood's egress? We generally don't want third-party egress.
[01:40] Aisha Patel: If you opt for Redwood-managed egress, we provide a published list of egress IP ranges and flow logs, plus signed attestations. However, many enterprise banks insist on full control, so the customer-owned NAT is typical. We also support IP allowlisting on our side for control-plane calls.
[01:54] Sofia Martinez: What about ingress — are customer requests proxied, or do we push data to Redwood?
[01:58] Jordan Lee: For our Private VPC product we prefer customer-originated requests to the model runtime in your VPC, so your internal services call the runtime over private networking. For hosted API it's outbound to Redwood; for private it's internal traffic. Aisha, do you want to show the sample VPC diagram?
[02:12] Aisha Patel: Sure — I'll describe verbally and we'll share the diagram after. Imagine three subnets: control plane subnet (private endpoints to Redwood control services), runtime subnet (model nodes, no internet access), and a management subnet for monitoring/ops bastions. Control plane communication is strictly over mTLS and mutual auth; we do not put keys in plaintext.
[02:30] Marcus Hale: mTLS — where are certs provisioned? We need to rotate certs using our PKI ideally.
[02:36] Aisha Patel: We support customer-managed certs and integration with your PKI. For the runtime, certs are mounted from a secrets store; for control plane we can exchange CA-signed certs. Rotation is supported via our orchestration, you can trigger rolling cert updates.
[02:50] Daniel Cho: How about firewalling and IDS/IPS — can Redwood integrate with our existing IDS?
[02:55] Aisha Patel: Yes. For cloud VPC, we recommend network-level IDS/IPS (like your existing vendor) at the egress/ingress chokepoints. We emit VPC Flow Logs and application-level audit logs that can be forwarded to your SIEM (we support syslog, TLS endpoints, and S3 buckets for ingestion). For on-prem, we can install an agent that forwards logs to your collectors.
[03:16] Sofia Martinez: Regarding log retention, what defaults do you have and can you configure retention windows?
[03:20] Aisha Patel: Out of the box we store audit logs for 90 days on the control plane, but for enterprise deployments we support custom retention with longer archival to your S3/GCS buckets or your SIEM. We can also provide immutable log exports for QSA auditing.
[03:34] Marcus Hale: Important for us: we need immutable audit trails for access to PII and the ability to show who invoked what model and with which dataset.
[03:42] Jordan Lee: Our audit trail records tokenized request/response metadata, caller identity (via SSO/RBAC principal), model version, and timestamps. Response payloads containing customer PII are only retained if you elect to; by default for Private they stay within your VPC and are not shipped to Redwood's hosted storage unless explicitly enabled.
[03:56] Daniel Cho: How are identities mapped — we use Okta for SSO and have groups mapped to role-based policies.
[04:02] Aisha Patel: We integrate with SAML/OIDC for SSO and support SCIM provisioning. RBAC is enforced via roles we define (admin/operator/readonly) and you can map Okta groups to those roles. We also support attribute-based access controls for more granular policies.
[04:18] Sofia Martinez: Data residency: if we deploy in our EU account, can you confirm no data crosses into US regions?
[04:24] Aisha Patel: Yes — for Private deployments the runtime and persistent storage live entirely in your account/region. Control plane can be customer-managed or we can provide a regional control plane; we have a regionalized control plane option for EU only. We'll confirm specifics in the architecture doc.
[04:38] Marcus Hale: Encryption at rest — we need customer-managed KMS and HSM-backed keys for any persistent caches and model artifacts.
[04:46] Aisha Patel: We support integration with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and HSM-backed keys. Data at rest for models, KV cache snapshots, and any persistent storage can be encrypted using customer keys. For ephemeral caches in memory, we rely on process isolation plus OS-level protections; nothing is written to disk unencrypted.
[05:06] Daniel Cho: What about secrets — where are API keys, DB creds stored?
[05:10] Aisha Patel: Secrets are stored in the customer-managed secrets store if you prefer (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager) and mounted at runtime as needed. We also support Redwood-managed secrets vault with customer KMS encryption, but for high security we recommend customer-managed stores.
[05:24] Jordan Lee: Quick interruption — Marcus asked earlier about blocking telemetry; do we send any outbound telemetry or phoning home?
[05:30] Aisha Patel: We do send limited telemetry for product health by default, but for Private deployments you can opt out entirely. We can run in a 'no-phoning-home' mode where all telemetry is pushed to your collector endpoints only; Redwood will not receive telemetry.
[05:44] Marcus Hale: Good. That helps with our compliance checklist. Next, network egress specifics: we have a strict allowlist and egress firewall. How do you handle outbound DNS/HTTP from model runtime during inference?
[05:55] Aisha Patel: During inference, the runtime should not make arbitrary outbound calls. Any external calls (for tool-calls or web access) are disabled by default. If you enable external tool calling, we require an explicit allowlist of domains and ports and provide instrumentation to monitor those calls.
[06:12] Sofia Martinez: For model updates/pulls, will nodes pull images from Redwood registries? That could create egress to public registries.
[06:18] Aisha Patel: For Private deployments, images can be mirrored to your internal artifact registry (ECR/GCR/AzureAcr) so nodes pull internally. We have automation to mirror and sign images; we also support an air-gapped image bundle for fully offline on-prem installs.
[06:33] Daniel Cho: Great. On firewalling, we need to validate rules at the PoC. Can Redwood run a pre-flight checker against our route table/NACLs to ensure connectivity?
[06:41] Aisha Patel: Yes — we have a connectivity validator script that you can run which reports on route tables, SGs, and NAT configs. We'll include that in the VPC template we share.
[06:51] Marcus Hale: Can you go into how you separate tenants and logs — we want proof that tenant A cannot access tenant B data even at a metadata level.
[06:58] Aisha Patel: Multi-tenancy for Private is achieved via strict namespace isolation at the orchestration layer, disk encryption with per-tenant keys, and RBAC scoping. Audit logs include tenant id and are stored immutably under customer-managed buckets. We also provide cryptographic separation for keys so there's no shared KMS key across tenants unless explicitly configured.
[07:19] Jordan Lee: If I can jump in: we also offer a canary/rollout approach where model traffic is routed by policy; for strict separation you can pin specific models to dedicated runtime pools per tenant.
[07:29] Sofia Martinez: About penetration testing and vulnerability management — do you provide the results or a schedule?
[07:35] Aisha Patel: We run quarterly internal pentests and annual external pentests. For enterprise customers we can provide summaries and remediation tickets; full reports can be shared under NDA. We also share our patch cadence and CVE response SLAs.
[07:49] Marcus Hale: Good. On compliance artifacts — we need SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 cert, and a list of subcontractors.
[07:57] Jordan Lee: We'll send the SOC 2 Type II report and our ISO letter. Subcontractor list will be included in the vendor security doc. Expect those docs in the email after this call.
[08:06] Daniel Cho: One technical detail — KV cache memory and off-heap storage: is any cache swapped to disk during OOM? We have rules preventing sensitive data from being written to ephemeral disk.
[08:16] Aisha Patel: The runtime keeps KV cache in memory; we don't swap to disk by design. If you enable large offload persistence for long-term caching, that storage is encrypted with your keys and we surface controls to scrub or avoid persisting sensitive tokens.
[08:30] Sofia Martinez: For IDS integration, do you provide standardized log mappings (like CEF/LEEF) to feed into our SIEM?
[08:36] Aisha Patel: Yes — we can export logs in CEF, LEEF, JSON over TLS, or S3 bucket exports. We'll include sample parsers for common SIEMs like Splunk and Sumo.
[08:48] Jordan Lee: I want to talk about network flow for initial onboarding: we will need a temporary admin VPC peering or a private link to set up the control plane; after that we can close that path if you want. Is that acceptable?
[09:00] Marcus Hale: It might be acceptable for setup; we need a checklist and justification for the temporary peering. We also require proof of certificate exchange and ephemeral keys.
[09:08] Aisha Patel: We'll provide a setup runbook that includes certificate exchange, ephemeral tokens, and exactly which ports/IPs are needed during provisioning. You can revoke anything after provisioning.
[09:18] Daniel Cho: Regarding network egress IP rotation — if we use our NAT, it's fine. If we used Redwood egress pool, how often do those rotate and how would we handle allowlists?
[09:28] Aisha Patel: Our managed egress pool publishes a set of static ranges for a minimum contract period; we can commit to notification windows for rotation and provide signed attestations. But again, customer NAT is recommended for strict allowlisting.
[09:41] Sofia Martinez: Any SLA or contractual guarantees around data locality and egress?
[09:46] Jordan Lee: For Private deployments, we can contractually bind data residency and egress restrictions; that'll be part of the enterprise addendum. We'll work with legal on specifics.
[09:56] Marcus Hale: Logging detail: can we get a sample of what the audit event looks like? We need fields like principal, action, model_version, request_hash, timestamp, and whether payload was redacted.
[10:06] Aisha Patel: Yes — we'll include a sample audit event schema. We also support request hashing and deterministic redaction rules so you can prove chain-of-custody without exposing PII.
[10:18] Daniel Cho: About SSO — we want to use Okta SCIM to provision service accounts so App-level keys aren't floating around. Does Redwood support SCIM for service accounts?
[10:26] Aisha Patel: We support SCIM provisioning for user accounts and can map service accounts via Okta apps; we also support short-lived credentials via your STS for programmatic access.
[10:36] Marcus Hale: For the PoC we want three tests: 1) connectivity and firewall rule validation, 2) throughput/latency under our egress device, and 3) audit log completeness and SIEM ingestion. Can you run those?
[10:46] Jordan Lee: Absolutely. We'll provide test plan templates and runbooks. Aisha will own the PoC technical setup with your team.
[10:52] Aisha Patel: I'll also include our connectivity validator and a set of terraform templates to spin up VPC subnets with recommended SGs and route tables.
[10:59] Sofia Martinez: Regarding cost — any incremental cost for customer-managed NAT and KMS?
[11:04] Jordan Lee: No additional Redwood fee for using customer-managed NAT or customer KMS; those are cloud costs on your side. Redwood charges are for dedicated runtime capacity and the private control plane where applicable. We'll send cost estimates.
[11:16] Marcus Hale: One last question on data deletion — if we terminate the deployment, what's the process to ensure data is wiped and keys are revoked?
[11:24] Aisha Patel: We support a termination runbook: revoke keys, cryptographically delete customer keys (if managed by customer), zero out persistent volumes, and provide a certificate of deletion. For customer-managed KMS, once keys are disabled/destroyed, our data is irrecoverable.
[11:38] Daniel Cho: Good. We also need a clear SLA for incident response and notification windows.
[11:42] Jordan Lee: We'll include IR playbook and notification timelines in the vendor security pack. For enterprise customers we offer faster RTO/RPO SLAs as part of SLA addendum.
[11:52] Sofia Martinez: Thanks — this covers everything I wanted. Can we recap next steps?
[11:57] Jordan Lee: Sure. Recap: Jordan will email SOC 2 Type II and ISO artifacts plus vendor security pack. Aisha will send VPC templates, connectivity validator, and sample audit schema. Marcus will share OceanCrest network diagram and egress policy. We'll align on PoC week of April 6th and confirm dates in follow-up.
[12:16] Marcus Hale: Sounds good. We'll aim to have the network diagram and firewall rule set by April 1st.
[12:22] Jordan Lee: Great. Any final quick questions?
[12:25] Marcus Hale: None from me. Thanks everyone.
[12:28] Sofia Martinez: Thanks — appreciate the thoroughness.
[12:30] Jordan Lee: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and the calendar invite for the PoC.
